name: New York-Style Pizza Sauce
headnote: J. Kenji Lopez-Alt is after a cooked, heavily seasoned sauce for by-the-slice New York pies, balancing sweetness, acidity and heat over a herbal backbone, and thin enough to spread but thick enough that the slice survives being folded. He swaps one of the two tablespoons of olive oil for butter, borrowing from Marcella Hazan, for a rounder mouthfeel, and keeps her trick of simmering halved onion in the pot and discarding it; side-by-side tests also showed dried oregano matched fresh, which he explains by noting that herbs from hot, dry climates hold their flavour through drying, though basil has to go in as fresh sprigs. He walks through the five canned tomato products and settles on whole peeled tomatoes packed in juice, pureed at home, because diced are firmed with calcium chloride, crushed are unregulated, and puree and paste already taste cooked. The sauce then reduces by half over very low heat for about an hour, since high heat would add unwanted roasted notes.
comment_digest: The long-running argument is whether a cooked sauce can be called New York style at all. Several readers, including one who worked in a Manhattan pizzeria in the 1980s, insist the real thing is an uncooked puree of canned tomato seasoned with salt, oregano and garlic or onion powder that cooks on the pie; others who also worked in pizzerias say theirs was always cooked and that simmering melds the flavours. Sweetness is the other complaint: one reviewer found the sugar plus the simmered onion halves too sweet to repeat, while another suggests whole carrots in place of the sugar. Reported umami additions include a single dash of Worcestershire and a Parmesan rind dropped in the pot. One cook needed about 90 minutes rather than 60 to reduce by half, and several say not to throw the cooked onion away.
flags: Comments truncated at 'Read More'. Much of the review section is an argument about authenticity rather than usable feedback, and several readers appear to misread the method (one asks how to remove onion that is in fact left in halves). Vote counts are all zero.
